title: Diana of the Grove
summary: A month with Diana: the grove and lake at Aricia, the strange priest-king of Nemi, the Aventine temple and the slaves' holiday on the Ides of August, the moon and the crossroads, and the witches' Diana of the nineteenth century, each kept in its own place.
welcome:
This journey runs about a lunar month. You will learn who Diana was to the Latins and Romans, what happened in her grove at Nemi, how the Ides of August were kept, how she became the Diana of later witchcraft, and how people honour her now. There is a nine-night practice under the moon, a Roman-style opening rite and, at the end, a self-dedication.

It is a self-dedication, not an initiation. It does not make you a priestess of Nemi, a member of any coven, or an initiate of Stregheria or Dianic Wicca; those traditions have their own processes. What is open to everyone is what was always open: a lamp, a clean offering, a walk in a wild place, and a promise kept.
about: Diana is an old Italian goddess of woods, wild animals, women in childbirth and the light of the moon. Her greatest shrine was a grove beside Lake Nemi, near Aricia in the Alban Hills, where women came with torches and left thanks for safe births and healing, and where a runaway slave served as her priest until another killed him and took his place. In Rome her temple on the Aventine was a shared sanctuary of the Latin peoples, and its birthday on the Ides of August was a holiday for slaves. Romans matched her with the Greek Artemis, and later with Luna and Hecate, so she became the "three-formed" goddess of earth, sky and crossroads. In the Middle Ages churchmen condemned women who believed they rode out at night with Diana, and in 1899 Charles Leland published Aradia, presenting Diana as queen of the witches. Today she is honoured by Roman polytheists in the old manner and by many modern witches as a moon goddess. Both are real; they are not the same thing, and this journey tells you which is which.
notes: This journey uses the Roman form throughout: clean hands, head covered (capite velato), exact words read from a page, Janus first. It follows the common modern pattern of Janus first and Vesta last in prayer, with the first share of any food set aside for Vesta. The ancient sources disagree on Vesta: Cicero says prayer ends with her, while Ovid (Fasti 6.303–304) says she is addressed first. Choose one way and keep to it.

The "Nemoralia" is a modern name: it is not found in any surviving ancient source. Ancient writers speak of the Ides of August at Nemi and of Diana's day on the Aventine; the torches, the rest from work and the washing of hair are ancient, but the name and many modern details are not.

Leland's Aradia (1899) and the "witches' Diana" are a nineteenth-century source of disputed origin, not ancient Roman religion. Dianic Wicca (from the 1970s) is a modern women-centred tradition. This app is inclusive: Diana protects women, and trans women are women. Nobody needs a particular body to honour her.
The priest of Nemi won his office by killing his predecessor. That is history, told honestly here, and nothing in this journey imitates it. All rites are devotional; there are no curses.

Mugwort and wormwood, often listed for Diana, should not be taken internally in pregnancy, are harmful to cats and dogs, and their smoke irritates lungs. Use bay, a cypress sprig or plain water instead if in doubt.

stages.title: Into the grove
stages.intro: Begin with a short walk and a simple Roman greeting. Diana is a goddess of places outside the house, so before the rite, go somewhere with trees or open sky, even a city park or a balcony at night, and notice one wild thing.

practices.title: Five minutes outside
practices.instructions: On each of these two evenings, step outside for five quiet minutes. Find the moon if it is up, or a tree, or a patch of weeds that nobody planted. Say quietly: "Diana, lady of the woods, I see this." Then go home.
practices.prompt: What wild thing did I notice, and what did it feel like to greet it?

rite.title: Greeting Diana
rite.summary: Wash and veil, Janus first, light a torch-flame for Diana, offer clean water and a little bread and honey, and close with Vesta and a turn to the right.

ingredients.name: A bowl of clean water and a towel for your hands
A head covering: a scarf or a fold of cloth
A white or silver candle in a stable holder (her torch)
A cup of fresh, cold water for the goddess
A small piece of bread with a little honey, on a clean dish
A few grains of frankincense and a burner
A sprig of bay or cypress, or a fallen leaf from your walk
Your words written on a card

rite.preparation: Clear a small space on a shelf or table, ideally by a window. Read the words through until you can say them without stumbling: Roman prayer cared about the exact words, and if you trip, the custom was to begin again. Break off a crumb of the bread and set it aside on a separate saucer for Vesta, the first share of food.

steps.title: Wash and veil
steps.instructions: Wash your hands in the clean water and dry them. Cover your head with the cloth, as Romans did to pray.

steps.title: Janus first
steps.instructions: Light the incense and give a few grains to Janus, the god called first, who opens every door.
steps.spoken:
Father Janus, opener of the way,
be honoured by this incense,
and open the way to Diana.

steps.title: Light her torch
steps.instructions: Light the candle. In her grove, women carried torches to Diana; this is yours. Lay the sprig beside it.
steps.spoken:
Diana, lady of mountains and green woods,
of hidden glens and loud rivers,
Lucina to women in labour, Trivia at the crossroads, Luna in the night,
or by whatever name it pleases you to be called:
I greet you with this light.

steps.title: Offer
steps.instructions: Set down the cup of water and the bread with honey. Name each gift exactly.
steps.spoken:
Diana, be honoured by this clean water,
be honoured by this bread and honey.
Be willing and favourable to me and my household.
I have come to learn your ways.

steps.title: Keep silence
steps.instructions: Sit quietly with the flame for a few minutes. Let the room be still, as a grove is still.

steps.title: Vesta last, and turn
steps.instructions: Give a pinch of incense, or simply a word, to Vesta, last in prayer. Turn to your right, uncover your head, and put out the flame.
steps.spoken: Vesta, last as always: be honoured.

rite.closing: Leave the water and bread until morning. Then pour the water onto the soil of a tree or plant, and put the bread out for the birds or into the compost. Vesta's crumb goes the same way.
rite.safety: Never leave a candle or incense unattended; keep it away from curtains, pets and children. Keep incense smoke away from birds and anyone with asthma. Honey must not be given to infants under one year old. Bread left out should be out of reach of dogs if it contains raisins or onion.

stages.title: Groves, temples and the moon
stages.intro: Five lessons, about two days each: who Diana is; the grove at Nemi and its priest-king; the Ides of August; how she was and is worshipped, with her shrine; and the hard and later parts of her story, from the Canon Episcopi to Aradia and Dianic Wicca.

lessons.title: Who Diana is
lessons.summary: An Italian goddess of woods, women and light, matched with Artemis, Luna and Hecate.

sections.heading: An Italian goddess first
sections.body:
Diana is not simply the Roman name for Artemis. She was worshipped by the Latins and other peoples of central Italy before Greek myth reached them, in groves and at springs, and her oldest shrines were outside Rome: at Aricia by Lake Nemi, on Mount Tifata near Capua, and elsewhere. Her name is probably related to the old Latin words for the bright sky and daylight (dius, dies), the same root as in Jupiter's name, so she may have begun as a goddess of light. That fits her later moon role well, but the etymology is a scholar's reconstruction, not a certainty.

She was a goddess of the wild margins: woods, mountains, untamed animals. But she was also, and just as much, a goddess of women. Women prayed to her in childbirth, and her shrines are full of thanks for safe births and healed bodies.

sections.heading: Catullus's hymn
sections.body:
The best short picture of the Roman Diana is a hymn by the poet Catullus, written for a chorus of girls and boys (poem 34). It begins "Dianae sumus in fide / puellae et pueri integri": "we are in Diana's keeping, girls and boys unwed." It calls her the daughter of Latona and Jupiter, born by the olive on Delos, so that she might be "montium domina ... silvarumque virentium / saltuumque reconditorum / amniumque sonantum", "lady of the mountains and green woods, of hidden glens and sounding rivers".

Then comes the heart of it. To women in labour she is called Juno Lucina, "she who brings to light"; she is "potens Trivia", mighty goddess of the place where three roads meet; and she is Luna, shining with borrowed light. As the moon she measures the year in her monthly course and fills the farmer's house with crops. And Catullus ends, in the true Roman way: "sis quocumque tibi placet / sancta nomine", "be hallowed by whatever name pleases you."

sections.heading: Three forms
sections.body:
By the late Republic poets called her triformis, "three-formed": Diana on earth, Luna in the sky, Hecate below and at the crossroads. Statues of the triple Hecate-Diana stood at Roman crossroads. This is a real ancient idea, but it is a learned, partly Greek one that grew over time; the early Latin Diana of the grove was simply Diana. The modern Wiccan "maiden, mother and crone" is a different idea again, from the twentieth century, and should not be read back into Catullus.

Romans also told Artemis's Greek myths of her: the twin of Apollo, the hunter who punished Actaeon for seeing her bathe, the virgin who guards her own boundaries. Use these, but remember that they came to Italy from Greece.

sections.heading: Her signs
sections.body: Her images are the bow and quiver, the short hunting tunic, the crescent on her brow and the torch. Her animals are the deer and the hunting dog. Her trees are the oak and laurel of her groves, and the cypress. Her places are woods, lakes, springs and crossroads. Her offerings were clean and simple: water, fruit, cakes, torches, garlands, and thank-offerings of small clay figures. Her colours today are white and silver.

knowAndDont.known: Catullus 34 (quoted above from the Latin) shows the Roman Diana as wild goddess, Lucina, Trivia and Luna together. Her Italian shrines at Aricia and Tifata, and her early Aventine temple in Rome, are attested by Livy, inscriptions and archaeology.
knowAndDont.unknown: What the Latins believed about Diana before Greek influence is mostly lost. The derivation of her name from "bright sky" is likely but not proven. The triple goddess as "maiden, mother, crone" is modern; the ancient triformis was Diana, Luna and Hecate.

lessons.inPractice: Learn the last line of Catullus's hymn in Latin or English and add it to the end of your prayers to her: "sis quocumque tibi placet sancta nomine", "be hallowed by whatever name pleases you."
reflect: Which of her faces draws me most: the woods, the women's goddess, the crossroads, or the moon?
What does it mean to me that she is both wild and a protector of births?
further: Catullus 34 (Latin at The Latin Library; public-domain translations on Gutenberg)
C. M. C. Green, Roman Religion and the Cult of Diana at Aricia (2007)

lessons.title: The grove at Aricia and the King of the Wood
lessons.summary: Lake Nemi, the torches, the votive gifts, Egeria and Virbius, and the runaway slave who served as Diana's priest.

sections.heading: Diana's mirror
sections.body:
In the Alban Hills south-east of Rome lies a small round lake in an old volcanic crater, Lake Nemi. It came to be called Diana's mirror (speculum Dianae), and the woods around it were her grove, nemus, which gives the place its modern name. Her sanctuary stood on the lake shore below the town of Aricia. It was a shared shrine of the Latin peoples: Cato the Elder recorded that the grove was dedicated by Egerius Baebius of Tusculum, a "Latin dictator", on behalf of several towns.

Ovid describes it in the Fasti (3.263–272): "vallis Aricinae silva praecinctus opaca / est lacus, antiqua religione sacer", "girt by the shady wood of the Arician valley is a lake, holy with ancient religion." Threads hang down covering the long fences, he says, and many a tablet is set up for the goddess who deserved it. "saepe potens voti, frontem redimita coronis, / femina lucentes portat ab Urbe faces": "often a woman whose prayer was granted, her brow crowned with garlands, carries shining torches from the City."

sections.heading: What people left
sections.body:
Excavations at Nemi have found thousands of gifts: small clay models of wombs, breasts, feet, eyes and hands, figures of mothers with babies, and statuettes of the goddess. These are thank-offerings and requests for healing and safe childbirth. Women walked the thirty-odd kilometres from Rome with torches; Ovid's line is a scene people would have known.

Two other powers lived in the grove. Egeria, a water nymph whose spring fed the lake, was said to have advised King Numa and to help women in childbirth. Virbius was a minor god identified with Hippolytus, the chaste Greek hero killed when his horses bolted, whom Diana had restored to life and hidden here; for that reason, Ovid says, no horses were allowed in the grove.

sections.heading: The King of the Wood
sections.body:
Diana's priest at Nemi was called the rex Nemorensis, "king of the grove". Ovid gives the rule in one line: "regna tenent fortes manibus pedibusque fugaces, / et perit exemplo postmodo quisque suo", "the strong of hand and swift of foot hold the kingship, and each later dies by his own example." The ancient writers Strabo and Servius explain: the priest was a runaway slave who had broken a branch from a particular tree in the grove and then killed the previous priest in single combat. He held office until someone killed him in turn. Suetonius says the emperor Caligula, finding the current priest had held on too long, set a stronger man to challenge him.

In 1890 James Frazer opened his huge book The Golden Bough with this priest, and built from him a theory of dying-and-rising god-kings across the world. Frazer's book was enormously influential, including on early modern witchcraft, but scholars now reject most of its comparisons. The rex Nemorensis was a real and strange local custom; what it meant to the Latins is not known.

sections.heading: Why it matters for practice
sections.body: Nemi shows Diana as a goddess people walked to, carried light for, and thanked with gifts that showed exactly what she had healed. It shows that her worship was full of women and their bodies, and also that it held a hard, violent edge that nobody has to reproduce. A modern devotee can keep the torches, the garlands, the written thanks and the walk, and leave the sword where it lies.

knowAndDont.known: Ovid, Fasti 3.263–272 (verified in Latin) describes the lake, the threads, the tablets, the torch-bearing women and the rule of the priesthood. Strabo (5.3.12) and Servius (on Aeneid 6.136) describe the slave-priest and the branch; Suetonius (Caligula 35) tells the Caligula story. The votive finds are in museums, notably at Nottingham and Rome.
knowAndDont.unknown: Why the priest had to be a runaway slave and win by killing, and what the branch meant, are unknown; Frazer's explanation is now largely rejected. Which tree the branch came from is not reliably recorded. The connection of Virbius with Hippolytus is a Greek-influenced story laid over a local god.

lessons.inPractice: Make a small votive for Diana in the Nemi manner: write on a card exactly what you thank her for or ask of her, plainly, and leave it on her shrine. If you are thanking her for healing, you can draw the part of you that was healed, as the women of Nemi modelled theirs in clay.
reflect: What would I carry a torch thirty kilometres to give thanks for?
How do I feel about the violence of the King of the Wood sitting beside the gentle gifts of the women?
further: Ovid, Fasti 3.259–276 (Latin at The Latin Library; Frazer's Loeb translation of 1931 and Riley's 1851 prose)
C. M. C. Green, Roman Religion and the Cult of Diana at Aricia (2007)
James Frazer, The Golden Bough, chapter 1 (1890; read as a classic of its time, not as current scholarship)

lessons.title: The Ides of August
lessons.summary: Diana's day on the Aventine, the slaves' holiday, the torches of Nemi, and how to keep 13 August.

sections.heading: The Aventine temple
sections.body:
Livy says King Servius Tullius persuaded the Latin peoples to build a shared temple of Diana in Rome, on the Aventine hill, after the model of the great temple of Artemis at Ephesus that the cities of Asia had built in common (1.45). Whether or not a king really founded it, the temple was very old and stood for the alliance of the Latins. Its birthday, the day it was dedicated, fell on the Ides of August, 13 August.

The Aventine was outside the old sacred boundary of Rome and was the hill of the plebs, the common people, and of outsiders. Diana's temple there had a special connection with the lowest people in Roman society. The scholar Festus records that the Ides of August were a festival of slaves, servorum dies festus, because King Servius, said to be the son of an enslaved woman, had dedicated the temple that day.

sections.heading: All Italy keeps the day
sections.body:
The poet Statius, writing in the first century AD, gives the most beautiful picture of the day (Silvae 3.1.55–60). In the fiercest heat of summer, when the Dog Star burns the fields, "fumat Aricinum Triviae nemus et face multa / conscius Hippolyti splendet lacus": "Trivia's grove at Aricia smokes, and the lake that knows Hippolytus's secret shines with many a torch." Diana herself "coronat / emeritos Diana canes et spicula terget / et tutas sinit ire feras": "crowns her hard-working hounds, wipes clean her arrows, and lets the wild beasts go safe." And "omnisque pudicis / Itala terra focis Hecateidas excolit idus": "and all the land of Italy keeps the Ides of Hecate at its chaste hearths."

So the day was a truce. The huntress herself stops hunting, the dogs are honoured, the animals are left alone, and every household keeps the festival at its hearth.

sections.heading: Washing the hair
sections.body: Plutarch, in his Roman Questions (100), asks why on the Ides of August slaves, men and women, have a holiday, and why women make a point of washing and cleansing their heads. He offers the Servius Tullius story as one explanation. The detail is small and lovely: it is a day of rest and of making oneself clean and new, especially for those who usually did the work.

sections.heading: Keeping 13 August now
sections.body:
Modern devotees, who often call the day the Nemoralia, keep it with candles or lanterns, often carried outdoors or floated on water in a safe bowl, rest from work where they can, wash their hair, garland their dogs, and leave fruit, garlands and written prayers for Diana. Many give to a women's refuge, a domestic-workers' or migrants' support group, or a wildlife charity, which fits both the slaves' holiday and the beasts let go safe.

A simple household form: rest as much as you can. Wash your hair in the morning. In the evening, wash and cover your head, give incense to Janus, light candles for Diana (several if you can, safely, in a group on a tray), offer water, fruit and a small cake, and read your written thanks aloud. Give your dog a treat and a ribbon. Do not hunt or fish. Name Vesta last.

knowAndDont.known: Livy 1.45 (verified in Latin) on the Aventine temple; Statius, Silvae 3.1.55–60 (verified in Latin) on the torches, the hounds and the Ides of Hecate; Festus on the slaves' holiday and Plutarch, Roman Questions 100, on the hair-washing (both paraphrased).
knowAndDont.unknown: The name "Nemoralia" is not attested in the ancient sources we have. Whether the Nemi festival and the Aventine anniversary were originally the same feast is debated. Floating candles, written prayers left at the shrine and many other modern customs are modern, if fitting.

lessons.inPractice: Put 13 August in your calendar now. Choose the charity or act of care you will dedicate to Diana that day, and write it down.
reflect: Who does the hard, unseen work in my life or my city, and how could I honour them on Diana's day?
What would a true day of rest look like for me?
further: Statius, Silvae 3.1 (Latin at The Latin Library; Mozley's 1928 Loeb translation)
Plutarch, Roman Questions 100 (Babbitt's Loeb translation on LacusCurtius)

lessons.title: Honouring Diana, then and now
lessons.summary: The Roman manner of prayer, her offerings, the moon and the Ides, modern communities, and how to set up her shrine.

sections.heading: The Roman manner
sections.body:
Roman prayer has a definite shape, and Diana is approached in it like any other god. Wash your hands. Cover your head with a fold of cloth (capite velato). Give incense or wine first to Janus, who opens. Then name the goddess, with her titles, and add "or by whatever name it pleases you to be called", as Catullus does. Name the gift exactly. Ask her to be "willing and favourable" (volens propitia) to you and your household, and make your request or give your thanks. Give the gift with the words "be honoured by this" (macte esto). Close with Vesta, turn to your right and uncover.

Romans read important prayers from a written text, and Pliny says that a word left out or said in the wrong order spoiled the rite. Write your prayer and read it. If you stumble, begin again from the start. That is not superstition; it is attention.

This journey follows the common modern pattern: Janus first and Vesta last in prayer, with the first share of food to Vesta. The ancient writers disagree (Cicero has Vesta last, Ovid has her first), so whichever you choose, keep it consistent.

sections.heading: Her offerings
sections.body:
Give Diana clean and simple things. Fresh water, ideally from a spring or at least cold from the tap, poured into a clean cup. Fruit, especially apples, pears and late-summer fruit. Small cakes and bread with honey. Garlands of leaves and flowers. Light: a candle, a lantern, a torch. Written thanks, like the tablets at Nemi. Her offerings, as a goddess of the upper world, can be shared: you may eat the fruit afterwards, or give it to the birds.

The gift she is most often asked for today is care for wild places and for the vulnerable: an hour clearing litter from a wood, a donation to a wildlife rescue, help for a woman leaving a violent home. Dedicate it aloud: "Diana, this is for you."

sections.heading: The moon and the Ides
sections.body: In the earliest Roman calendar the Ides of each month marked the full moon. They later became fixed dates (the 13th, or the 15th in March, May, July and October) and were sacred to Jupiter. Modern devotees often honour Diana as Luna at each full moon, and Roman polytheists may also keep the Ides. Either is reasonable; say which you are doing. Monday, the moon's day, belongs to the late Roman planetary week and suits her too.

sections.heading: Setting up her shrine
sections.body: Put it near a window that sees the sky if you can. You need a white or silver candle in a safe holder (her torch), a clean cup for water, a small dish for fruit or cake, and something from a wild place: a fallen oak leaf, an acorn, a pine cone, a stone from a river. A small image of the huntress, a deer or a hound, or a crescent moon, is optional. Add a box or envelope for your written thanks. Keep it clean and give it fresh water often.

knowAndDont.known: The Roman prayer form (veiled head, Janus first, exact words, "willing and favourable", "macte esto", turning right) is attested by Cato, Livy, Pliny (Natural History 28.10–11) and others. Votives, fruit, garlands and torches for Diana are attested at Nemi and in Ovid.
knowAndDont.unknown: Exactly how private Romans prayed to Diana at home is barely recorded. Full-moon worship of Diana as a monthly practice is a modern habit, built on her ancient identification with Luna. Charity as offering is a modern extension of old ideas.

lessons.inPractice: Set up her shrine this week and write your own short prayer to her in the Roman shape. Read it from the page each time you use it.
reflect: What feels natural to me in the Roman form, and what feels strange?
What act of care for a wild place or a vulnerable person could I offer her each month?
further: Mary Beard, John North and Simon Price, Religions of Rome (1998)
John Scheid, An Introduction to Roman Religion (2003)

lessons.title: Queen of the witches: later Dianas
lessons.summary: The Canon Episcopi, Leland's Aradia, Stregheria and Dianic Wicca: what they are, where they come from, and where this app stands.

sections.heading: Riding with Diana
sections.body:
Around the year 906, the church writer Regino of Prüm recorded a text later called the Canon Episcopi. It condemned certain wicked women who believed they rode out at night on beasts with "Diana, goddess of the pagans", crossing great distances and obeying her as their mistress. The church said these were illusions sent by the Devil. The text was copied for centuries, and Diana became the name that churchmen gave to a night-riding goddess of women in popular belief, whatever local name that figure really had.

This tells us something real about medieval folk belief, and something about how learned men used an old Roman name to describe it. It does not show that Roman Diana-worship survived in secret.

sections.heading: Leland's Aradia
sections.body:
In 1899 the American folklorist Charles Godfrey Leland published Aradia, or the Gospel of the Witches. He said it came from a Tuscan woman he called Maddalena, who gave him a manuscript of witch lore. In it Diana is the queen of witches, who sends her daughter Aradia to earth to teach witchcraft to the poor and oppressed against their masters and the church. The book influenced the first Wiccans in the 1950s, and lines and themes from it entered Wiccan liturgy.

Nobody knows how much of Aradia is genuine Italian folk tradition, how much was Maddalena's own composition, and how much was Leland's. No manuscript has been found. Scholars such as Ronald Hutton treat it as a fascinating nineteenth-century text, not evidence of ancient religion. You can love it, and many do, as long as you call it what it is.

sections.heading: Modern traditions
sections.body:
Stregheria, "witchcraft" in Italian, is a modern tradition largely shaped by the writer Raven Grimassi from the 1980s, drawing on Leland and on Italian folk magic; its claims to unbroken antiquity are disputed. Dianic Wicca began in the 1970s, notably with Zsuzsanna Budapest, as a women-centred, goddess-only tradition rooted in feminism. Some Dianic groups have excluded trans women, which has caused real hurt and argument; other Dianic and goddess communities welcome all women. Roman polytheists, meanwhile, honour Diana in the reconstructed Roman manner and generally keep the witch-Diana separate.

This app is inclusive. Diana guards women and the vulnerable, and that includes trans women and anyone whose body or life has been treated as not counting. Nobody needs a particular body, gender or ancestry to honour her.

sections.heading: What not to do
sections.body: Do not present Aradia or Wiccan moon rites as ancient Roman practice. Do not imitate the King of the Wood or treat the slave-priesthood as romantic. Do not take mugwort or wormwood internally without medical advice, and never in pregnancy. Do not hunt, fish or harm animals as an offering on her day. And do not invade the privacy of others in her name: Actaeon's story is about a boundary that should not be crossed.

knowAndDont.known: The Canon Episcopi appears in Regino of Prüm's collection of about 906. Leland's Aradia was published in London in 1899. Dianic Wicca and Stregheria are documented modern movements of the 1970s and 1980s onward.
knowAndDont.unknown: Who the night-riding goddess of medieval belief really was, and how far it reflects pre-Christian religion, is debated. The origins of Aradia, and whether Maddalena existed as Leland described, are unknown.

lessons.inPractice: Decide which Diana you are dedicating to: the Roman goddess of grove and temple, the witches' queen of later tradition, or both, held side by side and labelled honestly. Write a sentence about it in your journal.
reflect: What draws me to the witch-Diana, and what to the Roman one?
Who are the vulnerable people I would want Diana to protect, and how can I act for them?
further: Charles Godfrey Leland, Aradia, or the Gospel of the Witches (1899; public domain)
Ronald Hutton, The Triumph of the Moon (1999), on Leland and early Wicca
Carlo Ginzburg, Ecstasies: Deciphering the Witches' Sabbath (Italian 1989; English 1991), on the night-riding goddess

practices.title: Fresh water for Diana
practices.instructions: Through the study stage, keep a cup of fresh water on her shrine and change it each morning, pouring the old water onto a plant or tree. Say "Diana, be honoured" as you do.
practices.prompt: Did I remember? What did I learn about her today?

stages.title: Nine nights under the sky
stages.intro: Nine nights of light, water and attention to the wild. Roman religion knew nine-day rites (the novendiale), but this nine-night frame is a modern devotional form. If you can, start it so that it ends near the full moon or the Ides.

practices.title: Nightly torch and water
practices.instructions:
Each night: step outside or to an open window for a few minutes and look for the moon, or the darkest patch of sky. Come back in, wash your hands and cover your head. A grain of incense or a word to Janus. Light Diana's candle and say your written prayer to her, ending "be hallowed by whatever name pleases you". Pour fresh water into her cup. Sit for five minutes. Name Vesta last, turn to your right, uncover, and put the flame out.

On one of the nine nights, offer fruit and a small honey cake. On another, do one act of care for a wild place or an animal, and tell her about it.
practices.prompt: What was the moon or the sky like tonight? What wildness, in the world or in me, did I notice?

practices.title: A written votive
practices.instructions: Once in the nine nights, write a thank-you to Diana as the women of Nemi did: exactly what you thank her for, or what you ask. Leave it on her shrine.
practices.prompt: What do I most want to thank her for?

stages.title: Is she your goddess?
stages.intro: Take a few days to weigh what you have learned. Diana is a goddess of freedom; she does not keep anyone who would rather go. Stopping, pausing, or choosing another goddess or path is a good outcome, and so is staying a friend of hers without a formal dedication.

practices.title: Three evenings by her light
practices.instructions: Light her candle and answer the questions below in your journal, a few each evening.
practices.prompt: What have the nine nights shown me about Diana and about myself?

questions: Am I drawn to the Roman Diana of grove and temple, the witches' Diana, or both? Can I keep them honestly distinct?
Can I keep a regular practice for a year: fresh water, a monthly offering, 13 August?
What act of protection for women, the vulnerable or the wild am I actually willing to do in her name?
How do I feel about the hard parts of her history: the slave-priest, the church's use of her name, the arguments within Dianic communities?
Does the formal Roman manner feel right to me, or would I rather honour her more simply?
Is this a passing attraction to the moon and the huntress image, or a real wish for a relationship?

stages.title: The dedication
stages.intro: If you go ahead, hold this rite on a full moon, on an Ides, or on 13 August. It is a self-dedication, not an initiation: it does not make you a priestess, a witch of any lineage, or a member of any tradition that has initiations of its own. It takes the Roman shape of a vow (votum): you promise what you will do, and fulfil it.

rite.title: Self-dedication to Diana
rite.summary: A walk, purification and veil, Janus first, many lights, a vow read from the page, offerings of water, fruit, honey cake and a written votive, and Vesta last.

ingredients.name: A bowl of clean water and a towel
Several white or silver candles on a heatproof tray
A cup of fresh cold water
Fresh fruit and a small honey cake, on a clean dish
A garland or sprig of oak, bay or cypress leaves
A written votive for the shrine

rite.preparation: Earlier in the day, walk somewhere green and gather one fallen thing: a leaf, an acorn, a stone. Wash your hair, as Roman women did on Diana's day. Write your vow: your name; that you dedicate yourself to Diana as her devotee; for how long (a year is wise); and what you will do, such as fresh water on her shrine, a monthly offering, keeping 13 August, and a named act of care for the wild or the vulnerable. Read it aloud until it flows. Set aside a crumb of the cake for Vesta.

steps.title: Purify and veil
steps.instructions: Wash your hands and face. Put on clean clothes. Cover your head.

steps.title: Janus first
steps.instructions: Light the incense and give a few grains to Janus.
steps.spoken:
Father Janus, first in every prayer,
open the way to Diana.

steps.title: Light the torches
steps.instructions: Light the candles one by one, as the women of Nemi carried many torches. Lay the garland and the thing you gathered before them.
steps.spoken:
Diana, lady of mountains and green woods,
Lucina, Trivia, Luna,
guardian of women, of the young, of the wild beasts,
or by whatever name it pleases you to be called:
I come with light, as your people came to your grove.

steps.title: Read the vow
steps.instructions: Read your vow aloud, exactly. If you stumble, stop and begin again from the start.

steps.title: Offer
steps.instructions: Set down the water, the fruit and the honey cake, naming each. Place your written votive on the shrine.
steps.spoken:
Diana, be honoured by this clean water,
by this fruit and this honey cake,
by this light and these leaves.
Be willing and favourable to me and my household.
As I have vowed, so I will do.

steps.title: Keep silence
steps.instructions: Sit with the lights in silence. If you can see the moon, look at it.

steps.title: Vesta last, and turn
steps.instructions: Give a pinch of incense to Vesta. Turn to your right and uncover your head. Put out the candles one by one.
steps.spoken:
Vesta, last as always: be honoured.
Diana, be hallowed by whatever name pleases you.

rite.closing: Leave the offerings until morning, then pour the water at the foot of a tree and give the fruit and cake to the birds or the compost. Keep your vow on her shrine. Romans who fulfilled a vow set up an altar marked V.S.L.M., votum solvit libens merito, "paid the vow willingly, as was deserved"; at the end of your year, write those letters on your vow card and renew it.
rite.safety: Several candles together make real heat: use a metal or ceramic tray, keep them well apart, and never leave them unattended. Keep flames away from loose hair (tie it back once it is dry), sleeves and curtains. Keep incense smoke away from birds and anyone with asthma. Honey is not for infants under one. Keep cakes and fruit, especially grapes and raisins, away from dogs.

stages.title: Keeping faith with Diana
stages.intro: Her ongoing practice is light, water and care, with one great day in August and a monthly turn with the moon or the Ides. Rededicate once a year.

practices.title: Full moon or Ides
practices.instructions: Once a month, at the full moon or on the Ides (say which you keep), wash, veil, Janus first, light her candle, offer water and fruit or a cake, and read your prayer. Do your act of care for the wild or the vulnerable that month and tell her about it. Vesta last, turn right.
practices.prompt: What did I do for the wild or the vulnerable this month?

practices.title: The Ides of August
practices.instructions: On 13 August: rest from work if you can, wash your hair, garland your dog, and in the evening light many candles safely for Diana, offer water, fruit and a cake, and leave written thanks. Give to a women's refuge, workers' support group or wildlife charity. Rededicate by reading your vow again.
practices.prompt: What did this year with Diana give me, and what will I promise next?

practices.title: A walk for her
practices.instructions: Once a week, take a walk somewhere with trees, water or open sky, and greet her there. Pick up litter as you go.
practices.prompt: What did I see on the walk?
